samples.text:
The graph shows how much water was used in the world by agriculture, industry and domestic from 1900 to 2000.

Agriculture used the most water in all the time. In 1900 it used 500 km³ per year and in 1940 it was 900 km³. After 1940 it increased more faster, it reached 1,450 km³ in 1960 and 2,100 km³ in 1980. In 2000 it was 2,800 km³, which is the highest on the graph.

Industry used much less water than agriculture. It was only 40 km³ in 1900 and 120 km³ in 1940. Then it went up quickly to 330 km³ in 1960 and 720 km³ in 1980. But between 1980 and 2000 it only increased a little, to 790 km³.

Domestic use was the lowest. It started at 20 km³ and grow slowly until 1960, when it was 110 km³. After that it increased to 250 km³ in 1980 and 400 km³ in 2000.

Overall, all three sectors used more water in 2000 than in 1900, and agriculture was always the biggest user.
samples.why: Relevant but late overview · key features covered with chronological listing · adequate vocabulary with an inappropriate noun form · comparative, comma splice and tense errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The graph shows the amount of water used globally by the agricultural, industrial and domestic sectors over the twentieth century.

Overall, water consumption increased in all three sectors, and the growth became much faster after 1940. Agriculture was by far the largest user throughout the period, while domestic use remained the smallest.

In 1900, agriculture consumed 500 km³ of water per year, compared with just 40 km³ for industry and 20 km³ for domestic purposes. Agricultural use rose slowly at first, to 900 km³ in 1940, but then accelerated dramatically, reaching 2,100 km³ in 1980 and 2,800 km³ by 2000. This was more than five times the figure at the beginning of the century.

Industrial water use also grew relatively slowly until 1940, when it stood at 120 km³. It then increased rapidly to 720 km³ in 1980; however, the following twenty years saw only a small further rise, to 790 km³. Domestic consumption followed a steadier upward trend, climbing to 110 km³ in 1960 and then to 400 km³ in 2000, which represent a twentyfold increase over the whole period.
samples.why: Clear overview of growth and relative sizes · key features, including the industrial slowdown, highlighted · effective cohesion · appropriate vocabulary · generally accurate grammar with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The graph illustrates global water consumption, in cubic kilometres per year, by agriculture, industry and households between 1900 and 2000.

Overall, water use rose across all three sectors, with growth becoming markedly steeper from the middle of the century. Agriculture was consistently the dominant consumer, using more water than the other two sectors combined at every point, whereas domestic use remained the smallest.

At the start of the century, agriculture already accounted for 500 km³, compared with 40 km³ for industry and a mere 20 km³ for domestic use. Agricultural consumption grew gradually to 900 km³ by 1940, after which it soared, reaching 1,450 km³ in 1960 and 2,800 km³ in 2000.

Industrial use showed a similar acceleration after 1940, increasing sixfold from 120 km³ to 720 km³ between 1940 and 1980. Unlike the other sectors, however, it then levelled off, edging up to only 790 km³ by the end of the century. Domestic consumption, meanwhile, increased more steadily, although it too gathered pace in the second half of the period, more than doubling between 1960 and 1980 and rising to 400 km³ in 2000, twenty times its 1900 level.
samples.why: Skilful selection of key features, including the industrial plateau · clear overview · accurate figures with precise derived comparisons · wide, precise vocabulary · varied structures without errors.
